extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and aspiring poets/writers (early-18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and aesthetic principles for composing poetry, literary essays, and characterful epistolary pieces — emphasizing qualities of style, the conditions for creative work, and the balance of imagination and judgment that produces 'wit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virgilian poetic qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil is described as 'no one writing in so divine, so harmonious, nor so equal a Strain, which leaves the Mind composed, and softened into an agreeable Melancholy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim for a 'divine' harmony and an even, measured strain that composes and softens the reader's mind into a pleasing melancholy. The passage endorses calm, harmonious diction and a tempering of passion rather than violent extremes as an aesthetic ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two roads to poetic eminence (birth or diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct paths to the summit of the Muses: one 'guarded by the Genius which presides over the Moment of our Births' admitting only those 'on whom Melpomene had look'd with a propitious Eye' (innate gift); the other 'guarded by Diligence' which admits through laborious, intricate effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents a production/evaluation criterion: poetic greatness may arise either from natural genius (rare, immediate admission) or from persistent, arduous labour; a third, superior route combines both. Practical implication: lack of natural gift can be compensated by prolonged, disciplined effort, though it is more tedious and fewer persist to the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Fancy and Judgment to produce Wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy (imaginative, variable, sometimes extravagant) must be corrected by Judgment (gravity, correction of inconsistencies); their offspring is 'Wit', seated between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good writing/wit requires combining inventive imagination with sober critical taste. Fancy supplies novelty and variety ('continually varying her Dress'), while Judgment 'corrects her Inconsistences' and discards affected ornaments. Antipattern: unbridled Fancy without Judgment yields affectation and absurdity; too much Judgment without Fancy yields dryness. Aim for a measured synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitude, Silence, and Contemplation as conducive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The grove inhabited by Solitude, Silence, and Contemplation is depicted as the proper path toward the Mountain of the Muses; Solitude 'sat with her Arms across each other, and seemed rather pensive' and kept a 'celestial Globe, with several Schemes of Mathematical Theorems.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text endorses quiet, solitary reflection as a productive state for composing worthy works: remove distraction, cultivate silence and contemplation to be led towards higher inspiration. Antipattern: seeking immediate social applause or following vain intruders like Vanity and Lust who distract from true poetic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affectation as an (artful) device in persona and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the coquette's letter the author claims 'our greatest Charms are owing to Affectation' and links affectation to easily assumed mien, pensive attention at a tragedy, scornful approbation at a comedy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affectation can be a deliberate rhetorical or performative tool to produce charm and social effect in characters or narrators. As a compositional device, cultivated affectation can produce subtle social signals and comic or satirical effects. Antipattern: excess affectation becomes insipid or exposes vanity; use knowingly for characterization and social satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary realism and character-revealing detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator prints a private letter of a coquette as a means to 'alarm the World against her' — the letter's tone, particulars, and small social maneuvers (dance, chosen partners, mortifying rivals) reveal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using letters (or similar first-person documents) as a creative device, rely on authentic voice, concrete incidents, and social maneuvers to let character emerge indirectly. Rather than summarizing a personality, show it through a plausible epistolary persona and their actions; this is an effective method for satire and character study.
